choices.english: glorified together with the One who begot Him
choices.why: τῷ γεγεννηκότι is the Father who begot the Son. The concessive structure is kept: even though He serves as priest in His humanity, He is not outside the worship due to God.
rejected: the One who was born from among us

choices.why: θεσπέσιος, divinely inspired; Cyril's usual epithet for Paul and David.

choices.term: μόνος γὰρ ἐκ μόνου γεγέννηται τοῦ Πατρός
choices.english: He alone has been begotten of the Father alone
rejected: born alone from the Only-begotten of the Father

choices.term: καθεὶς ἑαυτὸν ἐν τοῖς καθ' ἡμᾶς ἐν πολλοῖς γέγονεν ἀδελφοῖς
choices.english: He lowered Himself into our condition and came to be among many brothers
choices.why: καθίημι, to let down; the clause echoes Romans 8:29 and explains 'Firstborn'.
rejected: each of us has become a brother to many

choices.term: παμμέγεθες τὸ μυστήριον, δέοιτ' ἂν ... μυσταγωγίας τῆς ἄνωθεν
choices.english: since the mystery is exceedingly great, it would rightly need instruction from above
choices.why: μυσταγωγία, initiation or instruction into a mystery, here from the Father.
rejected: since you have been brought into the experience of this mystery

choices.english: reaching from the Father through the Son to the creation
choices.why: διήκω, to extend through; the Spirit's mission, not His procession.
ἀπεοικώς, unlike or unfitting; the Son begotten of the Father's substance bears no unlikeness to Him.

choices.term: ὅλον ἑαυτὸν ... μονονουχὶ γράφοντος τοῦ Πατρός
choices.english: the Father all but writing His whole self into the nature of the Son
choices.why: μονονουχί, all but; genitive absolute with the Father as subject.

choices.term: τῷ πάντοτε θριαμβεύοντι ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ ... δι' ἡμῶν
choices.english: who always leads us in triumph in Christ and through us makes known
choices.why: The wording of 2 Corinthians 2:14, including 'through us'.

pass_a_gloss: [opens inside the quotation begun in the previous section: 'These things Isaiah said because he saw the glory'] of him, and spoke (λαλέω) about him.' Therefore even if the Father should be glorified (δοξάζω, opt. pass.) through him, and since he has been set (τίθημι, pf. pass.) 'a propitiation (ἱλαστήριον) through faith (πίστις)', and has also become 'minister (λειτουργός) of the holy [places]' on account of the human [nature] (τὸ ἀνθρώπινον), as a spiritual sacrifice (θυσία) he offers in priestly service (ἱερουργέω) the prayer (προσευχή) of each of the saints; for through him our amen; and he would not be understood (νοέω, opt. pass.) [as] outside the need (δεῖ) both to be worshipped (προσκυνέω, pass.) and to be glorified together (συνδοξάζω, pass.) with the one who has begotten (γεννάω, pf. ptc.) [him], at least by us ourselves and by the multitude (πληθύς) above of the holy spirits. And the inspired (θεσπέσιος) Paul said somewhere: 'And when again he brings (εἰσάγω) the firstborn (πρωτότοκος) into the inhabited world (οἰκουμένη), he says: And let all angels (ἄγγελος) of God worship him.' And yet to which of beings [is it] unclear (ἀσυμφανής) that he is Only-begotten (Μονογενής) in the respect in which he would be understood God? For alone (μόνος) from the Father alone has he been begotten (γεννάω, pf. pass.); but when, letting himself down (καθίημι) into our [condition], he came to be among many brothers (ἀδελφός), then he himself has been set first (πρωτεύω); and besides being Only-begotten as God, he has also been styled (χρηματίζω, pf.) firstborn on account of the human [nature]. 'And the one confirming (βεβαιόω) us with you into Christ, etc.' The God and Father confirms us into Christ, having founded (ἐνιδρύω, aor. mid.) a right (ὀρθός) and unshaken (ἀκατάσειστος) faith in the souls of all, persuading (ἀναπείθω) [them] to think (φρονέω) that he is God by nature and in truth, even if he should be seen in our form (σχῆμα), born according to flesh from a woman, the one above all creation (κτίσις); and indeed our Lord Jesus Christ himself, to Peter confessing (ὁμολογέω) the faith and saying clearly 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God', answered back (ἀντιφωνέω), saying 'Blessed (μακάριος) are you, Simon [col. 326] Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood did not reveal (ἀποκαλύπτω) [it] to you, but my Father who is in the heavens.' For since the mystery (μυστήριον) [is] exceedingly great (παμμεγέθης), it would fittingly need (δέομαι, opt.) initiation (μυσταγωγία) from above and from the Father; he himself therefore confirms us into Christ, the God who also sealed (σφραγίζω, aor. mid.) us and anointed (χρίω) [us] and gave the pledge (ἀρραβών) of the Spirit. And it would not be unclear to us through these things also, that the Son did not become 'yes and no', but rather true (ἀληθινός) God, and upon all the goods 'in him the yes'; for God being said to seal and anoint us, and having given the pledge of the Spirit, Christ again would be the one fulfilling (πληρόω) these things in us, not as a servant (ὑπουργικῶς), nor indeed anointing and sealing us with a foreign (ἀλλότριος) Spirit, but with his very own and the Father's; for in both [is] the Holy Spirit on account of the identity (ταυτότης) of the substance (οὐσία), not dividedly (μεμερισμένως), but as reaching through (διήκω) from Father through Son to the creation; for he breathed upon (ἐμφυσάω) the holy apostles saying: 'Receive Holy Spirit.' And through him and in him we have been sealed (κατασφραγίζω, pf. pass.) to the divine and intelligible (νοητός) image (εἰκών); for the divine apostle himself said, writing to the Galatians: 'My little children (τεκνίον), for whom again I am in birth pains (ὠδίνω) until Christ is formed (μορφόω, aor. pass.) in you.' And if, being formed into Christ, we are enriched with (πλουτέω) the divine imaging (εἰκονισμός) in ourselves, he himself therefore is the image of the God and Father and the exact (ἀκριβής) likeness (ἐμφέρεια), and not as we [are], called to likeness (ὁμοιότης) by participation (μέθεξις) of sanctification (ἁγιασμός), but rather by nature and essentially (οὐσιωδῶς); for the God by nature, toward the one by nature and truly God and begotten (γεννάω, pf. ptc.) from his substance, would have nothing unlike (ἀπεοικώς). And that he too has been sealed by the God and Father, John the most wise says: 'For the one having received his testimony (μαρτυρία) has sealed that God is true [col. 327].' And he has been sealed again not in equal manner (τρόπος) as we also, [stray numeral 3 omitted] but with the Father all but (μονονουχί) writing (γράφω) his whole self in the nature of the Son and as it were essentially imprinting (ἐνσημαίνω, mid.) [himself]; for this reason he said: 'The one having seen (ὁράω, pf.) me has seen the Father.' 'But thanks (χάρις) to God, the one always leading us in triumph (θριαμβεύω) in Christ and making manifest (φανερόω) the fragrance (ὀσμή) of the knowledge (γνῶσις) of him through us in every place.' The apostles give thanks (εὐχαριστέω) [cut off; continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: … and spoke about Him” (John 12:41). So even if the Father is glorified through Him, and since He has been set forth as “a propitiation through faith” (Romans 3:25), and has also become “a minister of the holy places” (Hebrews 8:2) because of His humanity, offering as a priest the prayer of each of the saints as a spiritual sacrifice (for through Him is our Amen), still He could not be thought to stand outside the duty of being worshiped and glorified together with the One who begot Him, both by us and by the multitude of holy spirits above.

The inspired Paul says somewhere, “And when He again brings the Firstborn into the world, He says, ‘Let all the angels of God worship Him’” (Hebrews 1:6). And yet to which of all beings is it unclear that He is Only-begotten insofar as He is understood to be God? For He alone has been begotten of the Father alone. But when He lowered Himself into our condition and came to be among many brothers (Romans 8:29), then He was set in the first place. So besides being Only-begotten as God, He has also been called Firstborn because of His humanity.

“Now He who establishes us with you in Christ,” and so on (2 Corinthians 1:21). God the Father establishes us in Christ by setting a right and unshaken faith in the souls of all, persuading them to hold that He is God by nature and in truth, even if He was seen in our form, He who is above all creation having been born of a woman according to the flesh. Indeed, when Peter confessed the faith and said plainly, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16), our Lord Jesus Christ Himself answered, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but My Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17). For since the mystery is exceedingly great, it would rightly need instruction from above, from the Father. So it is God Himself, who has also sealed us and anointed us and given us the pledge of the Spirit, who establishes us in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:21–22).

From these words too it should be clear to us that the Son did not become “yes and no” (2 Corinthians 1:19), but is rather true God, and that in all good things “in Him is the Yes” (2 Corinthians 1:20). For while God is said to seal and anoint us and to have given the pledge of the Spirit, it is again Christ who accomplishes these things in us, not as a servant, nor anointing and sealing us with a Spirit foreign to Him, but with the very Spirit that is His own and the Father’s. For the Holy Spirit is in both, because of the sameness of substance, not divided, but as reaching from the Father through the Son to the creation. For He breathed on the holy apostles, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22).

Through Him and in Him we have been sealed into the divine and spiritual image. For the divine apostle himself, writing to the Galatians, said, “My little children, for whom I am again in the pains of birth until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). And if, by being formed into Christ, we gain the riches of the divine image in ourselves, then He Himself is the image of God the Father and His exact likeness, not as we are, called to likeness by sharing in holiness, but rather by nature and in substance. For He who is God by nature can have nothing unlike Himself in the One who is God by nature and in truth and begotten of His own substance.

The most wise John says that He too has been sealed by God the Father: “For whoever has received His testimony has set his seal to this, that God is true” (John 3:33). Yet He has been sealed, again, not in the same way as we are, but with the Father all but writing His whole self into the nature of the Son and, as it were, imprinting Himself there in substance. That is why He said, “Whoever has seen Me has seen the Father” (John 14:9).
“But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and through us makes known the fragrance of the knowledge of Him in every place” (2 Corinthians 2:14). The apostles give thanks …
